transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-09 11:00 AM PT | Duration: 52 mins
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE - Security), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Liam Chen (CISO, CobaltBank), Sofia Martinez (Head of Platform), Raj Patel (Cloud Architect), Nina Alvarez (Compliance)

[00:00] Jordan Blake: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um, I'll kick off real quick, this is Jordan from Redwood, joined by Maya and Ethan. The goal today, quick security review focused on encryption, KMS options, and HSM/BYOK flow. Liam, Sofia, did I capture it right?

[00:18] Liam Chen: Yep that's right, thanks Jordan. We're primarily concerned about encryption in transit and at rest, and whether we can bring our own keys - also how audit logs look when keys are customer-managed.

[00:35] Maya Singh: Great, so at a high level Redwood encrypts data in transit with TLS 1.3 and at rest with AES-256. For model artifact and token storage we do envelope encryption - so the data keys are encrypted with a root key in a KMS. The options are: we manage the KMS key (default) or you bring keys into your cloud KMS (BYOK) or use an HSM-backed approach for additional assurance.

[00:55] Raj Patel: Quick clarification "when you say 'envelope encryption' can you explain where the data keys are stored and how rotation works?"

[01:05] Maya Singh: Sure. Data keys (DEKs) are generated per object/prefix and encrypted with a master key (KEK) — that master key lives in KMS. Rotation is handled by creating a new KEK and re-encrypting data keys on the fly or lazily during access; we support both immediate rewrap and lazy rewrap. There's also a key versioning scheme so you can audit which KEK version encrypted a given DEK.

[01:30] Nina Alvarez: And what about HSM? We have requirements that keys must be generated and never leave an HSM for certain regulated data.

[01:38] Maya Singh: Yep, supported. Two main patterns: cloud HSM + customer managed keys in your cloud KMS (e.g., AWS CloudHSM + KMS custom key store), or a dedicated HSM that your security team controls in a private deployment. For hosted Redwood we can integrate with your cloud KMS via a key policy and we never store plaintext root keys. For Private or Dedicated deployments, you can configure an on-prem HSM and Redwood will use the HSM for KEK operations. There are some network and latency considerations for HSM calls.

[02:05] Sofia Martinez: Latency is a concern — our SLAs are tight. HSM calls are slower, right? How do we mitigate without losing cryptographic guarantees?

[02:14] Ethan Park: Good question. We use envelope encryption specifically to avoid per-request HSM calls. Only the KEK unwrap/wrap operations hit the KMS/HSM. DEKs used for streaming inference are cached in a secure cache and rotated according to policy. So HSM call frequency is bounded — typically during key rotation or initial provisioning. That keeps steady-state latency low.

[02:40] Liam Chen: What about audit logs and key usage visibility? We need a tamper-evident audit trail showing key operations, who invoked them, and from where.

[02:51] Maya Singh: Redwood emits detailed audit events to the control plane, and when integrated with your KMS you'll get key usage logs natively (e.g., CloudTrail events for KMS in AWS). We can stream logs to your SIEM or to an S3 bucket in your account. For Private deployments all logs can stay in your VPC.

[03:12] Raj Patel: Is there any case where Redwood would hold plaintext keys?

[03:16] Jordan Blake: Short answer: no for production. We never persist customer KEKs in plaintext. For debugging in controlled scenarios we may decrypt in ephemeral memory during diagnostics but that's by exception and with strict controls — it's in our security docs. We'll share the exact wording in the artifact.

[03:35] Nina Alvarez: How do you handle key rotation policies? Can we force a rotation monthly and have Redwood enforce it?

[03:42] Maya Singh: Yes, you can enforce rotation cadence in KMS or via our admin APIs. We support automatic rotation windows and also provide an API to trigger rewrap across data keys. For large corpuses we do lazy rewrap to avoid huge migration windows.

[03:58] Sofia Martinez: Data residency — if we bring Redwood into a dedicated region, can we ensure keys and logs never leave the region?

[04:06] Maya Singh: For Dedicated/Private, yes. You can pin both the KMS key and log sinks to your region. For hosted multi-region, we can set region-level routing so requests for EU customers are routed to EU-hosted instances and EU KMS. We'll share our region boundary doc.

[04:25] Liam Chen: Can you talk about separation of duties and RBAC? Who in Redwood has access to key metadata vs actual usage?

[04:33] Maya Singh: We enforce least privilege. Redwood engineers don't have access to your KEKs. Our control plane can see key metadata (key IDs, rotation state) necessary for orchestration, but not plaintext. RBAC in the console maps to roles; we support SAML/SSO provisioning and SCIM for user sync. We can restrict who can request key operations via RBAC rules.

[04:56] Jordan Blake: Also want to call out support for customer-managed service accounts and KMS keys tied to those accounts — reduces blast radius.

[05:05] Raj Patel: One of our auditors asked about HSM attestation — do you provide attestation reports or can Redwood integrate with our HSM vendor to pull attestation?

[05:13] Maya Singh: We can provide HSM attestation artifacts when using cloud HSM — the cloud provider supplies the attestation. For on-prem HSMs in private deployments, you can surface your attestation or we can help attach it to onboarding docs. We'll include examples in the guide.

[05:29] Ethan Park: Another operational note: when configuring BYOK with AWS KMS custom key store, you need a KMS grant/policy that allows our service principal to use the key. We give the least-privilege policy snippet. For HSM-backed keys the grant is limited to Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey.

[05:50] Sofia Martinez: Are there any limitations on model caching or token caching when BYOK is enabled? Like, do you invalidate caches on rotation?

[05:58] Maya Singh: Caches are keyed by DEK version; when you rotate the KEK, we update DEK wraps; we can choose to invalidate caches or continue using cached DEKs until they expire. We usually recommend a short cache TTL during rotation windows. We'll include recommended TTLs in the guide.

[06:18] Liam Chen: For compliance, we need SOC2 Type II evidence and also ISO scope for the environment that will handle PII. Can you provide those?

[06:25] Jordan Blake: Yes — we'll send SOC2 and ISO artifacts. Note that for Private deployments the ISO scope can be adjusted based on the deployment.

[06:34] Nina Alvarez: One more — data deletion and key destruction. If we decommission keys, how do you ensure data is unrecoverable?

[06:42] Maya Singh: If KEKs are destroyed and you don't have backups, DEKs cannot be unwrapped and data is unrecoverable. For BYOK we recommend key lifecycle policies where you disable keys before schedule destruction and validate backups. We'll walk you through safe decommissioning steps.

[06:59] Raj Patel: Network architecture question — if we use cloud HSM, does Redwood require egress to your control plane for each inference?

[07:06] Ethan Park: No per-inference egress for key ops. We keep DEKs in a secured cache in the inference cluster. Only control plane operations and occasional rewraps may call out. For private deployments you can also run the control plane in your VPC to avoid external egress.

[07:26] Jordan Blake: Recap — Redwood supports TLS 1.3, AES-256 at rest, envelope encryption, BYOK via cloud KMS, HSM-backed KEKs, audit log streaming, RBAC/SSO, and private deployment options where keys and logs remain in your environment. Action items we'll follow up on.

[07:45] Sofia Martinez: Sounds good. We'll review the docs and get back on the POC timing. Thanks.

[07:52] Jordan Blake: Great, thanks everyone. We'll send materials after the call.

Notes / artifacts referenced:
- Link: Redwood security whitepaper + KMS integration guide (sent after call)
- Example KMS policy snippet and grant examples (Maya to share)
